decks.title: Cash Flow Statement — Part 1: Meaning, Cash Equivalents and Classification of Activities
goals: Explain what a cash flow statement is, why it is prepared and how profit differs from cash
Identify cash and cash equivalents and recognise what is not a cash flow
Classify cash flows into operating, investing and financing activities
Classify interest, dividends and income tax correctly for financial and non-financial companies

slides.heading: Cash Flow Statement
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what the statement shows, what counts as **cash and cash equivalents**, and how every cash flow is classified into **operating**, **investing** and **financing** activities.

nodes.label: What is not a cash flow

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: why cash is not profit, meaning and objectives, cash and cash equivalents, what is not a cash flow, the three activities and classifying transactions
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: A company can be profitable and still run short of cash. The cash flow statement tells us where cash came from and where it went during the year. In this part we learn what the statement is, what counts as cash and cash equivalents, and how every cash flow is sorted into one of three activities: operating, investing and financing.

slides.heading: Profit is not cash

rows: Less: Increase in trade receivables (not yet collected)
Less: Increase in inventories (cash tied up in stock)
Less: Part of a bank loan repaid

visual.alt: Table showing that an imagined company earned a profit of 3,00,000 yet its cash fell by 50,000, because customers had not paid, stock was built up, machines were bought and a loan was repaid
visual.caption: Profit is earned on the accrual basis; cash moves only when money is received or paid.

slides.narration: Meet Moyar Garments, an imagined company in Tiruppur. It earned a profit of rupees three lakh, yet its cash fell by rupees fifty thousand. Customers had not yet paid, stock had piled up, new machines were bought and part of a loan was repaid. Profit follows the accrual basis; cash moves only when money actually comes in or goes out. The cash flow statement bridges the two.

slides.heading: What is a cash flow statement?
bullets: Covers a period: inflows and outflows of **cash and cash equivalents**.

rows: the main revenue-earning business: customers, suppliers, employees, tax
buying and selling long-term assets and investments
raising and repaying owners’ capital and borrowings, interest and dividends paid
the increase or decrease in cash and cash equivalents
E, F. Opening and closing cash
the reconciliation with the two balance sheets

visual.alt: Table of the sections of a cash flow statement: operating, investing and financing activities, the net change, and the opening and closing cash and cash equivalents
visual.caption: Accounting Standard 3, Cash Flow Statements.

slides.narration: A cash flow statement shows the inflows and outflows of cash and cash equivalents during a period. Accounting Standard three requires the flows to be grouped into operating, investing and financing activities. Their total is the net change in cash, which must reconcile the opening balance with the closing balance in the two balance sheets.

slides.heading: Objectives of the statement

rows: Show the sources and uses of cash, activity by activity
Show whether operations generate enough cash
Explain the gap between profit and cash
Help plan future cash needs and repayments
Compare cash performance across years and firms

visual.alt: Table of objectives of the cash flow statement: sources and uses of cash, cash-generating ability of operations, the gap between profit and cash, planning, and comparison

slides.narration: Why prepare it? It shows the sources and uses of cash activity by activity. It tells lenders and shareholders whether the main business produces enough cash to pay its way. It explains why profit and cash differ. It helps management plan future cash needs and repayments. And because cash figures do not depend on accounting policies, it makes comparison between years and firms easier.

slides.heading: Quick check: the purpose
slides.body_md: Choose the main purpose of the statement.
slides.narration: Which statement explains the movement in cash, rather than profit or position?

slides.heading: Cash and cash equivalents
bullets: **Cash**: cash in hand and demand deposits with banks.
**Cash equivalents**: short-term, highly liquid investments, readily convertible into known amounts of cash, with an insignificant risk of change in value.

headers: Included in cash and cash equivalents
rows: Cash in hand; balances in current and savings accounts
Fixed deposits with more than three months to maturity when made
Treasury bills and commercial paper with three months or less to maturity when acquired
Equity shares, even if listed (value can change)
Short-term deposits maturing within three months

visual.alt: Table of what is and is not included in cash and cash equivalents: cash and bank balances and short-term investments maturing within three months are included; longer deposits, equity shares, receivables and inventories are not
visual.caption: Test: short-term, highly liquid, known amount of cash, insignificant risk of change in value.

slides.narration: Cash means cash in hand and money in current or savings accounts. Cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments that can be turned into a known amount of cash with little risk of a change in value. As a rule, they mature within three months of the date they are acquired: treasury bills, commercial paper and short deposits. Equity shares never qualify.

slides.heading: Quick check: the maturity test
slides.narration: How short must the maturity be, counted from the date the investment is acquired?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: cash and cash equivalents of Tapti Tiles
slides.body_md: Tapti Tiles Ltd (imagined, Surat) lists six holdings at the year end. Which of them are cash and cash equivalents?

rows: Treasury bills bought with 60 days to maturity
Fixed deposit maturing in five months
Commercial paper with 75 days to maturity when bought

visual.alt: Worked example table: of six holdings of an imagined tile company, cash in hand, the current account, sixty-day treasury bills and seventy-five-day commercial paper qualify, giving cash and cash equivalents of 2,40,000

slides.narration: Tapti Tiles, an imagined company in Surat, lists six holdings. Cash in hand and the current account are cash. Sixty-day treasury bills and commercial paper with seventy-five days to run are cash equivalents. The five-month fixed deposit is too long, and the listed shares can change in value. So cash and cash equivalents total rupees two lakh forty thousand.

slides.heading: Quick check: shares that sell in a day
slides.narration: Is being easy to sell enough to make an investment a cash equivalent?

slides.heading: What is not a cash flow

rows: Movement within cash and cash equivalents
Buying 60-day treasury bills from the bank balance
Shares issued to the seller of a building
Bonus shares out of the general reserve
Only as an add-back to profit

visual.alt: Table of items that are not cash flows: movements within cash and cash equivalents, non-cash investing and financing transactions, book transfers such as bonus shares, and non-cash charges such as depreciation

slides.narration: Some items never appear as flows. Moving money from the bank into a sixty-day treasury bill changes only the make-up of cash and cash equivalents, not their total. Issuing shares to the seller of a building, or issuing bonus shares, involves no cash at all; such non-cash transactions are disclosed in the notes instead. Depreciation is a non-cash charge: it appears only as an add-back to profit.

slides.heading: Three activities, one net change

nodes.label: Net change in cash and cash equivalents
Opening plus net change equals closing cash

visual.alt: Flow diagram: cash flows from operating, investing and financing activities add up to the net change in cash and cash equivalents, which reconciles opening and closing cash
visual.caption: Three activities, one net change

slides.narration: Every cash flow belongs to one of three activities. Operating activities are the main revenue-earning business. Investing activities are the purchase and sale of long-term assets and investments. Financing activities change the owners’ capital and the borrowings. The three totals add up to the net change in cash and cash equivalents, which reconciles the opening and closing balances.

slides.heading: Operating activities

rows: Cash sales; cash collected from customers
Payments to suppliers for goods and services
Wages, salaries and other employee costs
Income tax paid (unless linked to investing or financing)

visual.alt: Table of operating activities: inflows from customers, royalties and fees, outflows to suppliers and employees and for income tax
visual.caption: Principal revenue-producing activities of the enterprise.

slides.narration: Operating activities are the principal revenue-producing activities of the business. Inflows include cash from customers and royalties or fees earned. Outflows include payments to suppliers and to employees. Income tax paid is also operating, because tax arises from the profit of the business and is hard to split among activities, unless it is clearly linked to an investing or financing transaction.

slides.heading: Investing activities

rows: Sale of land, buildings, machinery, vehicles, patents
Purchase of fixed assets and intangible assets
Sale of shares or debentures of other companies (not cash equivalents)
Loans and advances given to other parties

visual.alt: Table of investing activities: inflows from sale of fixed assets and investments and from interest and dividend received; outflows for assets, investments and loans given

slides.narration: Investing activities concern long-term assets and investments that are not cash equivalents. Buying land, machinery, vehicles or patents is an outflow; selling them is an inflow. Buying shares or debentures of other companies, or lending money to another company, is an outflow too. For a company that is not a financial enterprise, interest and dividend received are investing inflows.

slides.heading: Financing activities

rows: Issue of equity or preference shares (with any premium)
Repayment of long-term and short-term loans
Issue of debentures; long-term loans raised

visual.alt: Table of financing activities: inflows from shares, debentures and loans; outflows for repayment of loans, interest and dividends

slides.narration: Financing activities change the size and make-up of owners’ capital and borrowings. Issuing shares, with any premium, and issuing debentures or raising loans bring cash in. Repaying loans, and paying interest and dividends, take cash out. For a company that is not a financial enterprise, interest paid is treated as a cost of finance, so it sits here, beside dividends paid.

slides.heading: Interest, dividends and tax: whose business is it?

visual.alt: Table of how interest, dividends and income tax are classified: for a non-financial company interest and dividend received are investing and interest and dividend paid are financing; for a financial company all except dividend paid are operating; income tax is usually operating

slides.narration: For an ordinary trading or manufacturing company, interest and dividend received are investing, and interest and dividend paid are financing. For a bank or a lending company, lending is its main business, so interest received, dividend received and interest paid are operating. Dividend paid is financing for everyone. Income tax paid is usually operating.

slides.heading: Quick check: classify four transactions
slides.body_md: Match each transaction with its class.
slides.narration: For each transaction, ask: is it trading, a long-term asset, a change in capital or borrowing, or no flow at all?

slides.heading: Worked example 2: classifying the cash flows of Mahanadi Motors
slides.body_md: Mahanadi Motors Ltd (imagined, Cuttack) had nine cash transactions in the year. Classify them and find the total for each activity.

headers: Cash transaction of Mahanadi Motors Ltd (imagined)
rows: Cash paid to suppliers and employees
**Net increase in cash and cash equivalents**

visual.alt: Worked example table: nine cash transactions of an imagined company classified into the three activities, giving operating 2,90,000, investing (4,35,000), financing 2,32,000 and a net increase of 87,000

slides.narration: Mahanadi Motors, an imagined company in Cuttack, had nine cash transactions. Receipts from customers, payments to suppliers and staff, and tax paid are operating, a net inflow of rupees two lakh ninety thousand. Machinery bought and sold and interest received are investing, a net outflow of rupees four lakh thirty-five thousand. Shares issued, interest paid and dividend paid are financing, an inflow of rupees two lakh thirty-two thousand. Cash rose by rupees eighty-seven thousand.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Inflows and outflows of cash and cash equivalents, Accounting Standard 3
Short-term, highly liquid, maturity three months or less, insignificant risk
Switching between cash and cash equivalents; non-cash transactions
Main business, including income tax paid
Long-term assets, investments, interest and dividend received
Shares, debentures, loans, interest and dividends paid

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: the cash flow statement, cash equivalents, what is not a cash flow, and the three activities

slides.narration: To sum up: the cash flow statement explains the change in cash and cash equivalents during a year. Cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments maturing within three months. Switching between cash and cash equivalents and non-cash transactions are not flows. Every flow is operating, investing or financing, and interest and dividends are classified according to the kind of business.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Apply the **three-month** test from the date of **acquisition**; shares are never cash equivalents.
For a **non-financial** company: interest and dividend **received** are investing; **paid** are financing.
Income tax paid is **operating** unless clearly linked to another activity.
**Non-cash** transactions are left out of all three activities.
In a classification answer, write the **activity** and whether it is an **inflow** or **outflow**.
slides.narration: In the exam, apply the three-month test from the date of acquisition, and remember that shares are never cash equivalents. For an ordinary company, interest and dividend received are investing, and paid are financing. Income tax paid is operating. Leave non-cash transactions out completely. When you classify, name the activity and say whether the item is an inflow or an outflow.

decks.title: Cash Flow Statement — Part 2: Preparation by the Indirect Method
goals: Work out net profit before tax from the changes in surplus, reserves, dividends and the provision for tax
Adjust profit for non-cash items, non-operating items and working-capital changes to find cash from operating activities
Use working accounts for fixed assets, accumulated depreciation, investments and provision for tax
Prepare investing and financing sections and check the statement against the change in cash

slides.heading: Preparing the statement: the indirect method
slides.body_md: Part 2 — from two balance sheets and additional information to a complete **cash flow statement**, with the **cash check** at the end.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: start from net profit before tax, adjust non-cash and non-operating items and working capital, deduct tax paid, add investing and financing flows, and check against the change in cash
visual.caption: The indirect method, step by step

slides.narration: Now we prepare the statement. We are given two balance sheets and some additional information. We find the net profit before tax, adjust it to reach the cash from operating activities, use working accounts to find the investing and financing flows, and finish with a check: the net change must equal the change in cash between the two balance sheets.

slides.heading: Direct and indirect methods

rows: Deducts gross cash paid to suppliers, employees and for tax
Adjusts for non-cash items, non-operating items and working capital

visual.alt: Table comparing the direct and the indirect method: they differ only in how operating cash flow is worked out; investing and financing are the same
visual.caption: Accounting Standard 3 allows both; the CBSE syllabus uses the indirect method only.

slides.narration: Accounting Standard three allows two ways of working out cash from operating activities. The direct method lists gross cash received from customers and gross cash paid out. The indirect method starts from net profit before tax and adjusts it. The CBSE syllabus uses the indirect method only, so the direct method is just for awareness. Investing and financing sections are the same either way.

slides.heading: The format at a glance

rows: Add: non-cash and non-operating charges; Less: non-operating income
Add / Less: changes in current assets and current liabilities
**Cash generated from operations**; Less: income tax paid
**D. Net increase or decrease (A + B + C)**; add opening cash and cash equivalents

visual.alt: Skeleton format of a cash flow statement by the indirect method: operating section from net profit before tax to net cash from operating activities, then investing and financing sections, the net change, and opening and closing cash

slides.narration: Here is the shape of the statement. The operating section begins with net profit before tax, adds back and deducts the adjustments, reaches operating profit before working capital changes, adjusts for working capital, and deducts tax paid. Then come the investing and financing sections. The three totals give the net change, which, added to the opening cash, must give the closing cash.

slides.heading: Our case company: Sabari Spices Ltd

rows: Surplus in the Statement of Profit and Loss

visual.alt: Comparative balance sheet of the imagined Sabari Spices Ltd at the end of 2026 and 2025: totals 21,70,000 and 19,20,000; cash and cash equivalents rose from 1,90,000 to 2,05,000
visual.caption: An imagined company; current year first, as in Schedule III.

slides.narration: Meet Sabari Spices, an imagined company in Kumily. Its balance sheet total grew from rupees nineteen lakh twenty thousand to rupees twenty-one lakh seventy thousand, and its cash and cash equivalents rose from rupees one lakh ninety thousand to rupees two lakh five thousand. We also know that a machine was sold at a loss, some investments were sold at a profit, part of the bank loan was repaid and two dividends were paid.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: net profit before tax
slides.body_md: Sabari (imagined): surplus rose from ₹1,60,000 to ₹2,40,000; ₹50,000 transferred to general reserve; dividends paid ₹1,00,000; provision for tax made ₹90,000.

rows: Less: Opening balance of surplus (31 March 2025)
Add: Provision for tax made during the year

visual.alt: Working of net profit before tax of Sabari Spices: increase in surplus 80,000, plus transfer to reserve, dividends paid and provision for tax, gives 3,20,000

slides.narration: The balance sheet shows only the profit kept back. To rebuild net profit before tax, start with the increase in surplus, rupees eighty thousand. Add back what was taken out of profit: the transfer to general reserve and both dividends paid. That gives profit after tax of rupees two lakh thirty thousand. Add the provision for tax made this year, and net profit before tax is rupees three lakh twenty thousand.

slides.heading: Adjusting for non-cash and non-operating items

headers: Add back (reduced profit, no operating cash out)
Deduct (raised profit, not operating cash in)
rows: Profit on sale of fixed assets
Goodwill, patents or preliminary expenses written off
Loss on sale of fixed assets or investments

visual.alt: Table of adjustments to net profit before tax: add back depreciation, amortisation, write-offs, losses on sale and finance costs; deduct profits on sale and interest and dividend received

slides.narration: Next, undo the items in profit that are not operating cash. Add back depreciation and amortisation, write-offs, losses on selling assets or investments, and finance costs, because no operating cash left the business for them. Deduct profits on sale, interest received and dividend received, because they are either not cash from operations or belong to investing activities. The result is operating profit before working capital changes.

slides.heading: Working-capital changes
bullets: Compare each current item in the two balance sheets.
Provision for tax and short-term borrowings are **not** working-capital items here.

visual.alt: Table of the working-capital rule: an increase in a current asset is deducted and a decrease added; an increase in a current liability is added and a decrease deducted
visual.caption: Cash and cash equivalents, provision for tax and short-term borrowings are dealt with separately.

slides.narration: Then adjust for changes in current assets and current liabilities. If inventories or receivables rise, cash is tied up, so deduct the increase. If they fall, cash is released, so add. Current liabilities work the other way: a rise in trade payables means bills not yet paid, so add it; a fall means they were paid off, so deduct it.

slides.heading: Quick check: payables rise
slides.narration: If suppliers are owed more at the end of the year, has more or less cash been paid out?

slides.heading: Worked example 4: operating activities of Sabari
slides.body_md: Net profit before tax, the adjustments, the working-capital changes and tax paid, from the balance sheets and the working accounts.

rows: Add: Loss on sale of machinery
Add: Interest on long-term bank loan (finance cost)
Less: Profit on sale of non-current investments

visual.alt: Operating section of Sabari Spices: net profit before tax 3,20,000, operating profit before working capital changes 4,36,000, cash generated 3,71,000, tax paid 70,000, net cash from operating activities 3,01,000

slides.narration: For Sabari, net profit before tax of rupees three lakh twenty thousand, with depreciation, the loss on the machine and the loan interest added back, and the investment profit and dividend taken out, gives rupees four lakh thirty-six thousand. After the working-capital changes, cash generated from operations is rupees three lakh seventy-one thousand. Deducting tax paid of rupees seventy thousand leaves net cash from operating activities of rupees three lakh one thousand.

slides.heading: Working account: machinery at cost

rows: Accumulated depreciation A/c (on the machinery sold)
Statement of Profit and Loss (loss on sale)

visual.alt: Machinery account of Sabari Spices at cost: opening 12,00,000, closing 15,00,000; the machine sold leaves at cost against its accumulated depreciation, sale price and loss; purchases are the balancing figure, 4,00,000
visual.caption: Working account at cost.

slides.narration: Where did the depreciation, the loss and the purchase come from? Working accounts. Machinery is shown at cost. The machine sold, costing rupees one lakh, leaves the account against its accumulated depreciation of rupees forty thousand, the sale price of rupees fifty thousand and a loss of rupees ten thousand. The figure needed to reach the closing balance, rupees four lakh, is the machinery bought.

slides.heading: Working account: accumulated depreciation

rows: Statement of Profit and Loss (depreciation for the year, balancing figure)

visual.alt: Accumulated depreciation account of Sabari Spices: opening 3,00,000, transfer on sale 40,000, closing 3,60,000; depreciation for the year is the balancing figure, 1,00,000

slides.narration: The accumulated depreciation account starts at rupees three lakh. The depreciation on the machine sold, rupees forty thousand, is transferred out. To reach the closing balance of rupees three lakh sixty thousand, the depreciation charged this year must be rupees one lakh. That is the figure added back in the operating section.

slides.heading: Working account: provision for tax

rows: Statement of Profit and Loss (provision for the year)

visual.alt: Provision for tax account of Sabari Spices: opening 60,000 plus provision for the year 90,000 less closing 80,000 gives tax paid of 70,000

slides.narration: Tax works the same way. The provision for tax starts at rupees sixty thousand, and rupees ninety thousand is provided this year. The closing balance is rupees eighty thousand, so the tax actually paid is rupees seventy thousand. The provision was added back through net profit before tax; the tax paid is deducted at the end of the operating section.

slides.heading: Quick check: tax paid
slides.body_md: Work out the tax paid from the provision for tax.
slides.narration: Opening provision plus this year’s provision, less the closing provision, gives the tax paid.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: investing activities of Sabari
slides.body_md: Machinery bought (from the working account), machinery and investments sold (investments costing ₹50,000 sold for ₹60,000), dividend received ₹14,000.

rows: Proceeds from sale of non-current investments

visual.alt: Investing section of Sabari Spices: machinery bought 4,00,000, machinery sold 50,000, investments sold 60,000, dividend received; net cash used 2,76,000

slides.narration: Sabari bought machinery for rupees four lakh, an outflow. It received rupees fifty thousand for the old machine and rupees sixty thousand for investments that had cost rupees fifty thousand. The dividend received on investments is an investing inflow too. Net cash used in investing activities is rupees two lakh seventy-six thousand. Notice that the full sale prices appear here, while the loss and the profit were adjusted in the operating section.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: financing activities of Sabari
slides.body_md: Shares issued at a premium; part of the 10% bank loan repaid on 1 April 2025; interest on the balance; final and interim dividends paid.

rows: Proceeds from issue of equity shares (including securities premium)
Interest on long-term bank loan paid

visual.alt: Financing section of Sabari Spices: shares issued with premium, loan repaid, interest and two dividends paid; net cash used 10,000

slides.narration: Sabari issued shares with a premium, bringing in rupees two lakh twenty thousand. It repaid rupees one lakh of its bank loan at the start of the year, and paid interest of rupees thirty thousand on the rest. It also paid a final dividend and an interim dividend, rupees one lakh in all. Net cash used in financing activities is rupees ten thousand.

slides.heading: Quick check: match the treatment
slides.body_md: Match each item with its treatment in the statement.
slides.narration: For each item, ask what it did to profit and whether its cash belongs to another activity.

slides.heading: The complete statement and the cash check

rows: Add: Loss on sale of machinery
Add: Interest on long-term bank loan (finance cost)
Less: Profit on sale of non-current investments
Proceeds from sale of non-current investments
Proceeds from issue of equity shares (including securities premium)
Interest on long-term bank loan paid
**Net increase in cash and cash equivalents (A + B + C)**
Add: Cash and cash equivalents at the beginning of the year
**Cash and cash equivalents at the end of the year**

visual.alt: Complete cash flow statement of Sabari Spices: operating 3,01,000, investing (2,76,000), financing (10,000), net increase 15,000, opening cash 1,90,000, closing cash 2,05,000
visual.caption: The net increase equals closing minus opening cash: the cash check.

slides.narration: Put the three sections together. Operating activities brought in rupees three lakh one thousand; investing used rupees two lakh seventy-six thousand; financing used rupees ten thousand. The net increase is rupees fifteen thousand. Added to the opening cash of rupees one lakh ninety thousand, it gives rupees two lakh five thousand, exactly the closing cash in the balance sheet. If your statement does not agree, a figure is missing or misplaced.

sections.heading: 2. Cash, cash equivalents and cash flows
sections.body_md:
- **Cash:** cash on hand and demand deposits with banks.
- **Cash equivalents:** short-term, highly liquid investments that are readily convertible into known amounts of cash and subject to an insignificant risk of change in value. An investment normally qualifies only when it has a short maturity of **three months or less from the date of acquisition** (for example, treasury bills, commercial paper, short bank deposits, overnight money-market funds). **Equity shares are excluded**; preference shares bought shortly before a fixed redemption date may qualify.
- **Cash flows:** inflows and outflows of cash and cash equivalents.

**Not cash flows:**
- movements **between** items of cash and cash equivalents (buying a 60-day treasury bill from the bank balance), because the total does not change;
- **non-cash** investing and financing transactions (assets acquired by issuing shares, bonus shares, conversion of one security into another); they are excluded from the statement and disclosed elsewhere.

sections.heading: 3. Classification into three activities
sections.body_md:
**Operating activities** — the principal revenue-producing activities of the enterprise and other activities that are not investing or financing. Examples: cash from sale of goods and services, royalties, fees and commission; payments to suppliers and employees; income tax paid (unless specifically identified with investing or financing).

**Investing activities** — the acquisition and disposal of long-term assets and of investments not included in cash equivalents. Examples: purchase and sale of land, buildings, machinery, vehicles, patents and goodwill; purchase and sale of shares and debentures of other enterprises; loans and advances made to others (by a non-financial enterprise) and their recovery.

**Financing activities** — activities that change the size and composition of owners’ capital and borrowings. Examples: issue of shares and debentures; raising and repaying loans; payment of dividends and of interest (non-financial enterprise).

sections.heading: 4. Interest, dividends, tax and special cases
sections.body_md:
**Interest and dividends** are classified according to the nature of the enterprise:
- **Non-financial enterprise** (manufacturer, trader): interest and dividend received → **investing**; interest and dividend paid → **financing**.
- **Financial enterprise** (bank, lending company): interest paid, interest received and dividend received → **operating**, since lending is its principal business; dividend paid → **financing**.

**Income tax paid** is operating unless it can be specifically identified with an investing or financing activity.

**Short-term borrowings** (bank loan, cash credit) are treated in this chapter as financing activities.

A **classification answer** should name the activity and show whether the item is an inflow or an outflow; totals are then worked activity by activity (worked example 2).

sections.heading: 5. The format and the indirect method
sections.body_md:
Accounting Standard 3 permits the **direct method** (gross receipts and payments) and the **indirect method** for operating activities; the CBSE syllabus uses only the **indirect method**. Investing and financing sections are prepared in the same way under both.

**Step 1 — net profit before tax.** The balance sheet shows only the retained part of profit, so rebuild it:

Net profit before tax = (closing − opening surplus) + transfers to reserves + dividends paid during the year (final for the previous year and interim) + provision for tax made during the year.

If tax is paid and charged without a provision, add the tax charged instead. Extraordinary items are not in the 2026-27 syllabus, so the first line is simply "net profit before tax".

sections.heading: 6. Operating activities: adjustments, working capital and tax
sections.body_md:
**Step 2 — non-cash and non-operating items.**
- **Add:** depreciation and amortisation; goodwill, patents and other intangibles written off; loss on sale of fixed assets or investments; interest and other finance costs.
- **Deduct:** profit on sale of fixed assets or investments; interest received and dividend received (non-financial enterprise).
- The result is **operating profit before working capital changes**.

**Step 3 — working capital.** For each current asset (inventories, trade receivables including bills receivable, prepaid expenses): **increase → deduct, decrease → add**. For each current liability (trade payables including bills payable, outstanding expenses): **increase → add, decrease → deduct**. The result is **cash generated from operations**. Cash and cash equivalents, provision for tax and short-term borrowings are not part of this step.

**Step 4 — tax.** Deduct **income tax paid**, found from the provision for tax account (opening + provision for the year − closing). The result is **net cash from operating activities**.

sections.heading: 7. Investing and financing activities, working accounts and the cash check
sections.body_md:
**Working accounts** find the figures the balance sheets hide:
- **Asset account at cost** (with a separate accumulated depreciation account): the asset sold leaves at cost against its accumulated depreciation, the sale price and the profit or loss; **purchases** are the balancing figure.
- **Accumulated depreciation account:** opening + depreciation for the year − depreciation on the asset sold = closing; the **depreciation for the year** is usually the balancing figure.
- **Asset at written-down value:** opening + purchases + profit on sale = sale price + loss on sale + depreciation + closing.
- **Investments account:** opening + purchases + profit on sale = sale price + loss on sale + closing.

**Investing:** purchases (outflows) and full sale prices (inflows) of fixed assets, intangibles and investments; interest and dividend received.

**Financing:** proceeds of shares (including premium; excluding shares issued to vendors or as bonus) and of debentures and loans; repayments; interest paid (work it on the balance and period outstanding); dividends paid.

**The cash check:** net increase or decrease (A + B + C) + opening cash and cash equivalents = closing cash and cash equivalents. Each balance sheet line must be explained by exactly one entry.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Starting from net profit **after** tax, or forgetting to add back the **dividends** and **transfer to reserve** when rebuilding profit.
- Deducting the **provision** for tax instead of the **tax paid**.
- Showing the **book value** instead of the **sale price** under investing, or forgetting to adjust the profit or loss on sale in operating.
- Treating interest or dividend **received** as operating, or interest **paid** as operating, for a non-financial company.
- Reversing the working-capital rule (an increase in receivables is **deducted**).
- Including **non-cash** transactions (shares to a vendor, bonus shares) or counting a switch into **cash equivalents** as a flow.
- Taking a full year’s interest on a loan raised or repaid during the year.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: classifying one item, or one treatment (MCQ, assertion-reason).
- 3 marks: cash and cash equivalents; one section (operating, investing or financing); net profit before tax with the tax account.
- 4 marks: one section with working accounts, or classification with totals.
- 6 marks: a complete statement — net profit before tax 1, working notes 1, operating 1½, investing 1, financing 1, net change and check ½.

questions.stem_md: The board of an imagined company, Siang Tea Estates Ltd, asks its accountant why a cash flow statement is prepared in addition to the Statement of Profit and Loss. The main purpose of the cash flow statement is to show

options.text_md: how much profit the company earned during the year after tax
where cash and cash equivalents came from and how they were used during the period, activity by activity
the financial position of the company on the last day of the year
how the profit for the year has been divided between dividend and reserves

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** where cash and cash equivalents came from and how they were used during the period, activity by activity. Profit is measured on the accrual basis; the cash flow statement explains the movement in cash and cash equivalents by operating, investing and financing activities. The other options describe the Statement of Profit and Loss, the balance sheet and the appropriation of profit.

questions.stem_md: Kosi Cables Ltd, an imagined company in Purnia, holds the following at the year end. Which one is a cash equivalent under Accounting Standard 3?

options.text_md: Equity shares of a listed company bought to be sold next month
A bank fixed deposit that had five months to run when it was made
Trade receivables falling due within thirty days
A 91-day treasury bill bought on the day it was issued

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A 91-day treasury bill bought on the day it was issued. A cash equivalent is a short-term, highly liquid investment, readily convertible into a known amount of cash and subject to an insignificant risk of change in value, usually with a maturity of three months or less from the date of acquisition. Shares carry price risk, a five-month deposit is too long, and receivables are not investments.

questions.stem_md: During March, an imagined company, Teesta Valley Packaging Ltd, carried out four transactions through its bank account. Which one will NOT appear as a cash flow in its cash flow statement?

options.text_md: Buying 60-day commercial paper with surplus money in its current account
Paying its suppliers for packaging film bought on credit
Buying a new printing machine for its factory
Paying the final dividend for the previous year

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Buying 60-day commercial paper with surplus money in its current account. Moving money from cash into a cash equivalent changes only the make-up of cash and cash equivalents, not their total, so AS 3 does not treat it as a cash flow. The other three are operating, investing and financing outflows.

shown only as a financing inflow of ₹6,00,000

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** left out of all three activities, because no cash or cash equivalent changed hands. Investing and financing transactions that do not use cash or cash equivalents are excluded from the statement; they are disclosed elsewhere in the financial statements.

questions.stem_md: True or false? An imagined trading company, Rupnarayan Jute Traders Ltd, can report a healthy net profit for a year and still end the year with less cash and cash equivalents than it started with.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Profit is earned on the accrual basis; cash can still fall if customers have not paid, stock has piled up, assets were bought or loans were repaid. That gap is exactly what the cash flow statement explains.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Listed equity shares that an imagined company, Dhansiri Rubber Products Ltd, can sell on the stock exchange within a day are cash equivalents, because they are readily marketable.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Being easy to sell is not enough. Equity shares can change in value significantly and have no maturity date, so they fail the "insignificant risk of change in value" test of a cash equivalent.

questions.stem_md: An investment is normally treated as a cash equivalent only if it has a short maturity, of ___ months or less from the date of acquisition.
questions.solution_md: Accounting Standard 3 takes three months or less from the date of acquisition as the usual test of a short maturity.

questions.stem_md: In India, the cash flow statement of a company is prepared according to Accounting Standard ___ (Cash Flow Statements).
questions.solution_md: Accounting Standard 3, Cash Flow Statements, issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, sets out how the statement is prepared and classified.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Equity shares held by a company are not treated as cash equivalents even if they can be sold quickly.

**Reason (R):** A cash equivalent must be subject to an insignificant risk of change in value.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: share prices move, so the amount of cash the shares will fetch is not known in advance.

**Assertion (A):** An issue of fully paid bonus shares out of the general reserve does not appear in the cash flow statement.

**Reason (R):** Transactions that do not require the use of cash or cash equivalents are excluded from the cash flow statement.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true and R is the reason for A: a bonus issue only moves an amount from reserves to share capital, with no cash received or paid.

questions.stem_md:
Netravati Cashew Exports Ltd, an imagined company in Mangaluru, holds the following on 31 March 2026. How much of it is cash and cash equivalents (in ₹)?

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | ---: |
| Cash in hand | 25,000 |
| Balance in current account with a bank | 1,35,000 |
| 91-day treasury bills bought on their issue date | 60,000 |
| Fixed deposit with a bank, maturity one year | 2,00,000 |
| Commercial paper with 80 days to maturity when acquired | 40,000 |
| Equity shares of a listed company | 75,000 |
questions.solution_md: Cash and cash equivalents = 25,000 + 1,35,000 + 60,000 + 40,000 = 2,60,000, that is ₹2,60,000. The one-year deposit is too long and the shares carry price risk, so both are left out.

questions.stem_md:
The cashier of Shetrunji Salt Works Ltd, an imagined company in Bhavnagar, has listed what the company holds on 31 March 2026. Identify, with a reason for each, which items form part of cash and cash equivalents, and find their total.

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | ---: |
| Petty cash | 6,000 |
| Balance with a bank in current account | 94,000 |
| Bank deposit for 30 days | 50,000 |
| Bank deposit for six months | 1,20,000 |
| Units of an overnight money-market fund | 30,000 |
| Trade receivables | 80,000 |
| Equity shares held as a short-term investment | 45,000 |
questions.solution_md: Test each item against the three conditions: short maturity (three months or less), readily convertible into a known amount, insignificant risk of change in value.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Item | ₹ | Treatment |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Petty cash | 6,000 | **Included** (cash) |
| Balance with a bank in current account | 94,000 | **Included** (cash) |
| Bank deposit for 30 days | 50,000 | **Included** (equivalent: short maturity, fixed amount) |
| Bank deposit for six months | 1,20,000 | **Not included**: maturity longer than three months |
| Units of an overnight money-market fund | 30,000 | **Included** (equivalent: highly liquid, insignificant risk of change in value) |
| Trade receivables | 80,000 | **Not included**: an operating asset, not an investment |
| Equity shares held as a short-term investment | 45,000 | **Not included**: risk of change in value |

**Cash and cash equivalents** = 6,000 + 94,000 + 50,000 + 30,000 = **₹1,80,000**.

questions.stem_md: The owner-directors of an imagined family company, Kapila Silk Weavers Ltd, say: "We already prepare a Statement of Profit and Loss; a cash flow statement adds nothing." State any three objectives or uses of a cash flow statement that answer them.
questions.solution_md: Give three distinct objectives, each with a line on why the profit statement alone does not meet it.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Explains the change in cash:** it shows, activity by activity, how cash and cash equivalents were generated and spent, which the accrual-based profit figure cannot show.
2. **Judges the ability to generate cash:** cash from operating activities shows whether the business can pay suppliers, staff, interest, tax and dividends from its own trading, without borrowing or selling assets.
3. **Helps planning and decisions:** past flows help to forecast future cash needs, to plan repayment of loans and to decide on new investment and dividend policy.
4. *(Also accepted)* It allows comparison of cash performance between years and firms, since cash figures are not affected by different accounting policies; it helps lenders and investors judge liquidity.

questions.stem_md:
An imagined company, Mahananda Agro Exports Ltd, Siliguri, had these three transactions in 2025-26. Its trainee accountant has shown each of them in the cash flow statement. Explain why none of them should appear there as a cash flow.

(i) Issued equity shares of ₹5,00,000 to the seller of a cold-storage building as the purchase price.
(ii) Issued bonus shares of ₹2,00,000 out of the general reserve.
(iii) Bought 60-day treasury bills for ₹1,00,000 by cheque from its current account.
questions.solution_md: For each item ask two questions: did cash or a cash equivalent leave or enter the business, and did the total of cash and cash equivalents change?

answer.model_answer_md:
**(i) Shares issued for a building:** an investing transaction (buying an asset) and a financing transaction (issuing shares), but no cash moves. It is a **non-cash transaction**, excluded from the statement and disclosed in the notes.

**(ii) Bonus shares from reserve:** an amount is only transferred from the general reserve to share capital; nothing is received or paid. It is also a **non-cash** item.

**(iii) Treasury bills bought by cheque:** treasury bills of 60 days are themselves a **cash equivalent**. Money has moved from cash at bank into a cash equivalent; the total of cash and cash equivalents is unchanged, so it is **not a cash flow**.

marking_scheme.step: (ii) Bonus issue is a book transfer
(iii) Movement within cash and cash equivalents

questions.stem_md: A Class 12 student preparing a project on an imagined company, Pench Furnishings Ltd, has to explain four terms in her introduction. Explain the meaning of (a) a cash flow statement, (b) cash, (c) cash equivalents and (d) cash flows, giving an example of each where you can.
questions.solution_md: Define each term in the words of the standard and add a concrete example; note that switching between cash and cash equivalents is not a cash flow.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a) Cash flow statement:** a statement, prepared under Accounting Standard 3, that shows the inflows and outflows of cash and cash equivalents of an enterprise during a period, classified into operating, investing and financing activities, and reconciles the opening and closing balances. Example: Pench Furnishings reports that its cash rose by a stated amount because its trading brought in more than it spent on new machines.

**(b) Cash:** cash on hand and demand deposits with banks. Example: notes in the cash box and the current-account balance.

**(c) Cash equivalents:** short-term, highly liquid investments that are readily convertible into known amounts of cash and are subject to an insignificant risk of change in value, generally maturing within three months of acquisition. Example: a 91-day treasury bill bought on issue.

**(d) Cash flows:** inflows and outflows of cash and cash equivalents. Example: money received from a customer is an inflow; wages paid are an outflow. A movement between cash and a cash equivalent (buying a treasury bill with cash) is not a cash flow.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Meaning of a cash flow statement
(c) Cash equivalents with the three-month test

questions.stem_md: Damanganga Polymers Ltd, an imagined plastics manufacturer in Vapi, paid interest on its 9% debentures during the year. In its cash flow statement the interest paid is shown under

options.text_md: operating activities
investing activities
financing activities
none of the activities, being a non-cash charge

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** financing activities. For an enterprise that is not a financial enterprise, interest paid is a cost of obtaining finance, so it is a financing outflow; in the indirect method it is first added back to net profit before tax.

questions.stem_md: Hiran Marble Works Ltd, an imagined company in Jabalpur, received a dividend on the shares of another company that it holds as a long-term investment. For Hiran, this dividend received is

options.text_md: an investing inflow
an operating inflow
a financing inflow
a reduction of financing outflows

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** an investing inflow. For a non-financial company, interest and dividend received are returns on its investments and are classified as investing activities.

questions.stem_md: Purna Dairy Products Ltd, an imagined company in Parbhani, paid its income tax for the year in instalments. Unless the tax can be specifically identified with another activity, the tax paid is shown as

options.text_md: an outflow under financing activities
an outflow under investing activities
an appropriation, not shown in the cash flow statement
an outflow under operating activities

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** an outflow under operating activities. Taxes on income arise from the operations that earn the profit, and it is usually impracticable to split them among activities, so AS 3 classifies them as operating unless specifically identified with investing or financing.

questions.stem_md: Kali Sindh Finance Ltd, an imagined company in Jhalawar, is a finance company whose main business is lending money to farmers. Interest received by it on these loans is classified as

options.text_md: an investing activity
an operating activity
a financing activity
an operating activity only if received in cash on the due date

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** an operating activity. For a financial enterprise, lending and earning interest is its principal revenue-producing activity, so interest received (and interest paid, and dividend received) are operating; dividend paid is still financing.

questions.stem_md: Wainganga Paper Ltd, an imagined paper manufacturer, lent ₹3,00,000 for two years to Kanher Pulp Ltd, an imagined supplier, to help it modernise. In the cash flow statement of Wainganga Paper (not a financial enterprise), the loan given is

options.text_md: an outflow under investing activities
an outflow under operating activities
an outflow under financing activities
not shown, because it will be repaid

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** an outflow under investing activities. Cash advances and loans made to other parties by an enterprise that is not a financial enterprise are investing activities; their repayment later is an investing inflow.

questions.stem_md: Subansiri Couriers Ltd, an imagined courier company in North Lakhimpur, sold one of its old delivery vans for cash. The sale proceeds are shown in its cash flow statement under

options.text_md: operating activities, since vans are used in daily deliveries
investing activities
financing activities
operating activities as a non-cash adjustment

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** investing activities. Acquiring and disposing of long-term assets such as vehicles are investing activities, even when the asset is used in daily operations; any profit or loss on the sale is adjusted in the operating section.

questions.stem_md: A student is classifying four cash transactions of an imagined manufacturer, Sarju Steel Furniture Ltd. Match each transaction in column A with its class in column B.

options.text_md: Cash paid to suppliers of steel sheets
Cash paid for a new welding machine
Cash received from an issue of debentures
Purchase of 45-day treasury bills with cash

match_right.text_md: Not a cash flow (movement within cash equivalents)

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Day-to-day trading is operating; long-term assets are investing; changes in owners’ capital and borrowings are financing; a switch between cash and cash equivalents is not a flow at all.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Cash received by an imagined cement company, Bhima Cements Ltd, from selling shares of another company that it had held as a long-term investment is an investing inflow.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Acquisition and disposal of investments other than cash equivalents (and other than trading stock) are investing activities.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Dividend paid by a bank to its shareholders is shown under financing activities.

**Reason (R):** For a financial enterprise such as a bank, interest received and dividend received are operating activities.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but R does not explain A. A is true because dividend paid is a return to providers of capital for every kind of enterprise; R is about receipts, which for a financial enterprise come from its main business.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Income tax paid by a manufacturing company is generally classified as an operating activity.

**Reason (R):** Income tax is calculated on the profit before tax shown in the Statement of Profit and Loss.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but R is not the reason for A. The tax is classed as operating because it arises from the operations that earn the profit and is usually impracticable to identify with investing or financing activities.

questions.stem_md:
Classify the following cash transactions of Pench Furnishings Ltd, an imagined furniture maker in Chhindwara, into operating, investing and financing activities:

(1) Purchase of goodwill of a small rival business.
(2) Cash paid to suppliers of timber.
(3) Issue of 10% debentures for cash.
(4) Royalty received for a furniture design licensed to another maker.
(5) Interim dividend paid to shareholders.
(6) Loan given to another company (the company is not a financial enterprise).
questions.solution_md: Ask whether each item is part of trading (operating), relates to long-term assets or investments (investing), or changes the owners’ capital or borrowings (financing). Royalties and fees are trading receipts.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Transaction | Activity |
| --- | --- |
| Purchase of goodwill of a small rival business | **Investing** |
| Cash paid to suppliers of timber | **Operating** |
| Issue of 10% debentures for cash | **Financing** |
| Royalty received for a furniture design licensed to another maker | **Operating** |
| Interim dividend paid to shareholders | **Financing** |
| Loan given to another company (the company is not a financial enterprise) | **Investing** |

questions.stem_md: Two imagined companies share a building in Pune: Mula Gears Ltd, which makes gearboxes, and Mutha Housing Finance Ltd, which lends to home buyers. Show how each company would classify (i) interest received, (ii) dividend received, (iii) interest paid and (iv) dividend paid, and give the reason for the difference.
questions.solution_md: Fill the grid one enterprise at a time, then explain why the principal business of a lender changes the class of interest and dividend receipts and of interest paid.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Item | Mula Gears Ltd (not a financial enterprise) | Mutha Housing Finance Ltd (financial enterprise) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| (i) Interest received | Investing | Operating |
| (ii) Dividend received | Investing | Operating |
| (iii) Interest paid | Financing | Operating |
| (iv) Dividend paid | Financing | Financing |

**Reason:** for a lender, borrowing, lending and earning interest are its principal revenue-producing activities, so these flows are operating. For a manufacturer they are returns on investments or costs of finance. Dividend paid is a return to shareholders in both cases.

questions.stem_md:
Sharavati Tools and Dies Ltd, an imagined engineering company, had these cash flows in 2025-26. Find its net cash used in investing activities (write the amount without a minus sign).

| Cash flow | ₹ |
| --- | ---: |
| Purchase of machinery | 3,20,000 |
| Sale of old machinery (book value ₹50,000) | 45,000 |
| Purchase of patents | 60,000 |
| Sale of non-current investments | 1,10,000 |
| Interest received on debentures held as investment | 18,000 |
| Dividend received on shares held as investment | 7,000 |
| Dividend paid to shareholders | 50,000 |
| Income tax paid | 40,000 |
questions.solution_md: Investing items only: (3,20,000) + 45,000 − 60,000 + 1,10,000 + 18,000 + 7,000 = (2,00,000); net cash used in investing activities = ₹2,00,000. Dividend paid is financing and tax paid is operating; the book value of the machine sold is not a cash flow.

marking_scheme.step: Investing items selected with correct signs

questions.stem_md:
Kapila Silk Mills Ltd, an imagined company in Nanjangud, gives the following cash transactions for 2025-26. Calculate its net cash from financing activities.

| Transaction | ₹ |
| --- | ---: |
| Issue of equity shares at a premium of ₹40,000 (face value ₹4,00,000) | 4,40,000 |
| Repayment of a long-term bank loan | 1,50,000 |
| Interest paid on the long-term loan | 27,000 |
| Final dividend paid | 80,000 |
| Short-term bank loan raised | 50,000 |
| Interest received on fixed deposits held as investment | 12,000 |
| Purchase of looms | 2,10,000 |
questions.solution_md: Financing items: 4,40,000 − 1,50,000 − 27,000 − 80,000 + 50,000 = 2,33,000, that is ₹2,33,000. Interest received is investing for a non-financial company, and the looms are an investing outflow.

marking_scheme.step: Financing items selected with correct signs

questions.stem_md:
Sarju Steel Almirahs Ltd, an imagined manufacturer in Ayodhya, recorded the following cash transactions in 2025-26. Classify each into operating, investing or financing activities, and compute the net cash flow from investing activities and from financing activities.

| Transaction | ₹ |
| --- | ---: |
| (i) Bought a delivery van | 3,50,000 |
| (ii) Issued equity shares for cash | 5,00,000 |
| (iii) Received interest on investments | 20,000 |
| (iv) Paid the final dividend | 90,000 |
| (v) Sold old machinery | 60,000 |
| (vi) Paid wages to factory workers | 1,10,000 |
| (vii) Repaid part of a long-term bank loan | 1,00,000 |
| (viii) Paid income tax | 45,000 |
questions.solution_md: Classify first, attach the sign (inflow or outflow), then add within each class; wages and tax stay in operating activities.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Transaction | Activity | Inflow / (outflow) ₹ |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| (i) Bought a delivery van | **Investing** | (3,50,000) |
| (ii) Issued equity shares for cash | **Financing** | 5,00,000 |
| (iii) Received interest on investments | **Investing** | 20,000 |
| (iv) Paid the final dividend | **Financing** | (90,000) |
| (v) Sold old machinery | **Investing** | 60,000 |
| (vi) Paid wages to factory workers | **Operating** | (1,10,000) |
| (vii) Repaid part of a long-term bank loan | **Financing** | (1,00,000) |
| (viii) Paid income tax | **Operating** | (45,000) |

- **Net cash from financing activities** = 5,00,000 − 90,000 − 1,00,000 = 3,10,000, an inflow of **₹3,10,000**.

questions.stem_md: Explain to the new finance team of an imagined company, Sabarmati Denim Ltd, Ahmedabad, the three activities into which cash flows are classified under Accounting Standard 3. For each activity give its meaning and two examples of inflows and two of outflows, and state how Sabarmati, a manufacturer, should classify interest and dividends received and paid.
questions.solution_md: Give the standard’s meaning of each activity, then two inflows and two outflows from a denim manufacturer’s own business, and finish with the four interest and dividend items.

answer.model_answer_md:
**1. Operating activities** — the main activities through which Sabarmati earns its revenue, together with any activity that is neither investing nor financing.
- Inflows: cash received from customers for denim sold; royalties or commission received.
- Outflows: cash paid to suppliers of cotton yarn; wages and salaries paid; income tax paid (unless identified with another activity).

**2. Investing activities** — acquisition and disposal of long-term assets and of investments not included in cash equivalents.
- Inflows: sale proceeds of an old dyeing machine; proceeds from the sale of long-term investments.
- Outflows: purchase of new looms or land; purchase of shares or debentures of other companies; loans given to other parties.

**3. Financing activities** — transactions that alter the amount and the mix of the capital put in by the owners and of the money borrowed.
- Inflows: proceeds from issue of equity shares or debentures; long-term loans raised.
- Outflows: repayment of loans; dividends paid; interest paid.

**Interest and dividends at Sabarmati (not a financial enterprise):** interest and dividend received are **investing** inflows; interest and dividend paid are **financing** outflows.

marking_scheme.step: Interest and dividends received and paid classified

questions.stem_md: The accountant of an imagined company, Shetrunji Ceramics Ltd, prepares the operating section of its cash flow statement by the indirect method, as the CBSE syllabus requires. Her starting figure is

options.text_md: total cash received from customers, from which cash paid to suppliers and employees is deducted
the closing balance of cash and cash equivalents
net profit before tax, which is then adjusted for non-cash items, non-operating items and working-capital changes
net profit after tax and after transfer to reserves

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** net profit before tax, which is then adjusted for non-cash items, non-operating items and working-capital changes. The indirect method works back from net profit before tax to cash generated from operations. Listing gross receipts and payments (the second option) describes the direct method, which is not in the syllabus.

questions.stem_md: Between the two balance sheets of an imagined company, Mandakini Herbal Remedies Ltd, trade payables rose by ₹25,000. In computing cash from operating activities by the indirect method, this change is

options.text_md: deducted from operating profit, because liabilities have grown
shown under financing activities as borrowing from suppliers
ignored, because trade payables are not cash
added to operating profit, because suppliers have financed part of the purchases and less cash was paid out

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** added to operating profit, because suppliers have financed part of the purchases and less cash was paid out. An increase in a current liability means expenses or purchases were charged in the profit figure but not yet paid in cash, so it is added; a decrease would be deducted.

questions.stem_md: Prepaid expenses of Ken Valley Granites Ltd, an imagined company, fell from ₹18,000 to ₹10,000 during the year. In the operating section of its cash flow statement (indirect method) the change of ₹8,000 is

options.text_md: deducted, because a current asset has fallen
added under investing activities
deducted from net profit before tax as a non-operating item
added, because part of this year’s expense was paid for in cash last year

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** added, because part of this year’s expense was paid for in cash last year. A decrease in a current asset releases cash or, as here, means an expense charged this year needed no cash this year; so it is added back. An increase in a current asset is deducted.

questions.stem_md: Tawa Organics Ltd, an imagined fertiliser company, sold an old tractor with a book value of ₹80,000 for ₹65,000. How is this shown in its cash flow statement (indirect method)?

options.text_md: Loss of ₹15,000 deducted in operating activities; ₹80,000 shown as an investing inflow
₹65,000 shown as an operating inflow; nothing in investing activities
Loss of ₹15,000 added back in operating activities; ₹65,000 shown as an investing inflow
Loss of ₹15,000 added back in operating activities; ₹80,000 shown as an investing inflow

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Loss of ₹15,000 added back in operating activities; ₹65,000 shown as an investing inflow. The loss was charged in arriving at net profit but is not an operating cash outflow, so it is added back; the cash actually received, the sale price, is the investing inflow.

questions.stem_md: Surplus in the Statement of Profit and Loss of Siang Bamboo Products Ltd, an imagined company, rose from ₹1,50,000 to ₹2,30,000. During the year it transferred ₹40,000 to general reserve, paid a final dividend of ₹60,000 and made a provision for tax of ₹70,000. Its net profit before tax is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** ₹2,50,000. Net profit before tax = increase in surplus 80,000 + transfer to reserve 40,000 + dividend 60,000 + provision for tax 70,000 = 2,50,000. Leaving out the tax gives profit after tax; leaving out the appropriations understates profit.

questions.stem_md: The provision for tax of Rupnarayan Jute Mills Ltd, an imagined mill in Howrah, stood at ₹45,000 on 1 April 2025 and at ₹60,000 on 31 March 2026. The provision made for the year 2025-26 was ₹75,000. The income tax paid during the year was
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** ₹60,000. Provision for tax account: 45,000 + 75,000 − closing 60,000 = 60,000 paid. This tax paid, not the provision, is deducted in the operating section.

questions.stem_md: Dhansiri Rubber Moulders Ltd, an imagined company in Dimapur, shows machinery at cost of ₹6,00,000 on 31 March 2025 and ₹7,50,000 on 31 March 2026. During the year a machine that had cost ₹90,000 was sold. How much machinery was bought during the year?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** ₹2,40,000. In the machinery account at cost: opening 6,00,000 + purchases − cost of the machine sold 90,000 = closing 7,50,000, so purchases = 7,50,000 + 90,000 − 6,00,000 = 2,40,000.

questions.stem_md: Subansiri Bamboo Crafts Ltd, an imagined company, earned a net profit before tax of ₹3,00,000 after charging depreciation of ₹50,000 and interest on debentures of ₹24,000, and after crediting a profit of ₹12,000 on the sale of a vehicle and interest received of ₹8,000. Its operating profit before working capital changes is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** ₹3,54,000. 3,00,000 + 50,000 + 24,000 − 12,000 − 8,000 = 3,54,000: add back the non-cash charge and the finance cost, take out the non-operating gains.

questions.stem_md: When the operating section starts from net profit before tax and adjusts it for non-cash items, non-operating items and changes in working capital, the statement is prepared by the ___ method.
questions.solution_md: This is the indirect method, the one prescribed in the CBSE syllabus; the direct method lists gross cash receipts and payments instead.

questions.stem_md: Cash generated from operations, less income tax paid, gives the net cash flow from ___ activities.
questions.solution_md: Income tax paid is the last deduction in the operating section; what remains is the net cash flow from operating activities.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Goodwill of ₹20,000 written off by an imagined company, Kanhar Minerals Ltd, during the year is added back to its net profit before tax in the operating section.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Writing off goodwill is a non-cash charge, like depreciation and amortisation; it reduced profit without any cash leaving, so it is added back.

questions.stem_md: True or false? An imagined manufacturer, Ghatprabha Sugars Ltd, should add the interest received on its investments to net profit before tax in the operating section of its cash flow statement.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Interest received is already inside net profit, and for a non-financial company it belongs to investing activities, so it is deducted in the operating section and shown as an investing inflow.

questions.stem_md: Match each item from the records of an imagined company, Ib Valley Bricks Ltd, with its treatment in a cash flow statement prepared by the indirect method.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Depreciation is added back to net profit before tax in the indirect method.

**Reason (R):** Depreciation is a source of cash for the business.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: depreciation was deducted in arriving at profit but involves no cash outflow, so it is added back. R is false: depreciation does not bring in any cash; the cash came from revenue.

questions.stem_md:

**Reason (R):** An increase in trade receivables means that part of the revenue included in profit has not yet been collected in cash.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: the increase is deducted. R is true, and it is exactly why the increase must be deducted, since revenue in the profit figure was not received in cash.
